blocks.text: Every BST operation walks one path from the root, so its cost is the tree's **height** h — not its size. The same seven values can make a tree of height 3 or of height 7, depending only on the **order** they were inserted. Keeping h small is what "balanced" means, and it's the difference between O(log n) and O(n).

blocks.alt: The values 1 to 7 inserted in sorted order make a chain: each new value is bigger than everything so far, so it always goes right, and the height is 7. Inserted middle first, as 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7, the same values make a perfect tree of height 3.

blocks.text: How tall can a BST be?

items: **Best case — balanced:** each level holds twice as many nodes as the one above, so n nodes need only about **log₂ n** levels: 20 levels for a million values, 30 for a billion.

**Worst case — skewed:** values inserted in sorted (or reverse-sorted) order always go the same way, giving a chain of height **n**. Search, insert and delete become O(n) — no better than a linked list.
**Random order:** inserting values in random order gives an expected height of about **2.99 · log₂ n** — usually fine, but not guaranteed.
**Each node** stores its value plus two pointers (left and right): about 24–40 bytes in Java or C++ before the value itself — two to five times what the same values take in a plain array.
**The whole tree** is O(n) memory. Nodes live wherever the allocator puts them, so walking a BST has poor cache locality compared with scanning an array.
**Recursion** on a BST uses O(h) stack: tiny when balanced, but a recursive walk of a 100,000-node chain overflows most call stacks — use a loop or an explicit stack when the tree might be skewed.
**Morris traversal** visits the tree in O(1) extra memory by temporarily re-using empty pointers.

blocks.text: Checking whether a tree is balanced

A tree is **height-balanced** when, at every node, the heights of the two subtrees differ by **at most 1**. The direct way computes the height of both subtrees at every node — repeated work that costs O(n log n) on a balanced tree and O(n²) on a chain. The better way computes heights **bottom-up** in one post-order pass and stops as soon as a subtree is out of balance.

blocks.caption: Each node gets its height from its children's; a difference of 2 or more means unbalanced.

blocks.text: **Time O(n log n)** on a balanced tree, **O(n²)** on a chain: every node recomputes heights below it. **Space O(h).**
**Time O(n), space O(h).** Each node's height is computed once, from its children's.

**Self-balancing** BSTs check the shape after every insert and delete, and repair it with **rotations**: a rotation lifts a child above its parent while keeping the in-order sequence — and so the BST rule — exactly the same. Each rotation is O(1), so insert and delete stay O(log n).

blocks.alt: A right rotation at node 6, whose left child is 4. 4 moves up to 6's place, 6 becomes 4's right child, and 4's old right subtree, 5, becomes 6's left child. The in-order sequence, 2 4 5 6 7, is unchanged, and the left side is one level shorter.

elements.text: the child moves up; the in-order sequence doesn't change
elements.originalText: the child moves up; the in-order sequence doesn't change

blocks.code:
def rotate_right(node):
    up = node.left                    # the left child moves up
    node.left = up.right              # its right subtree moves across to node
    up.right = node                   # node becomes its right child
    return up                         # the new root of this subtree

items: **AVL trees** keep every node's subtree heights within 1 of each other — the strictest balance, so the fastest lookups.
**Red-black trees** allow a little more slack (no path more than twice as long as another) in exchange for fewer rotations — used by Java's `TreeMap` and C++'s `std::map`.
**B-trees** keep many keys per node and stay perfectly balanced; databases and file systems use them so each step reads one disk page.
**Without a self-balancing tree:** build from sorted data middle-first (Convert Sorted Array to BST), or rebuild an unbalanced tree in O(n) (Balance a BST) — both are problems later in this course.

blocks.alt: Balanced BST: search, insert, delete: O(log n) time, O(log n) space. Skewed BST: search, insert, delete: O(n) time, O(n) space. Check balance bottom-up: O(n) time, O(h) space.
